questions.question: Q: How has digital convergence changed audience behaviour?

points.text: Digital convergence (smartphones combining multiple media functions) means audiences can access all media forms on a single device, anywhere, anytime. This has changed behaviour: audiences expect on-demand content, switch between media forms seamlessly, and create as well as consume content. Traditional scheduled media consumption has been replaced by personalised, portable media experiences.

questions.question: Q: What are the ethical concerns of AI in media?

points.text: AI raises concerns about: deepfakes (realistic but fake video/audio) undermining trust in media; algorithmic bias reinforcing stereotypes; automated content replacing human creativity; data collection for AI training without consent; and personalisation creating filter bubbles that limit diverse perspectives. Each of these challenges requires regulatory and ethical responses.

questions.question: Q: Evaluate the impact of streaming on media consumption habits.

points.text: Streaming has created binge-watching culture, on-demand viewing, and personalised recommendations. Audiences expect content when and where they want it. However, algorithms create filter bubbles, the sheer volume of content creates 'choice paralysis', and the attention economy raises addiction concerns. Overall, streaming has increased convenience but also created new problems.

markScheme.exemplarAnswer: Digital technology has transformed how audiences access, consume, and participate in media, creating both empowerment and new vulnerabilities. The most significant change is the shift from scheduled to on-demand consumption. Streaming services allow audiences to watch what they want, when they want, on any device. This gives audiences unprecedented choice and control over their media experience. Social media enables participation — audiences are now prosumers who create and share content as well as consuming it. However, this control is partly illusory. Algorithms determine what content appears in feeds and recommendations, creating filter bubbles where audiences see content that reinforces their existing views. The attention economy designs platforms to maximise engagement, using psychological techniques (autoplay, notifications, infinite scroll) that can lead to compulsive use. This is particularly concerning for younger audiences. Digital technology has also increased access to diverse content. Audiences can discover global media, niche interests, and alternative voices that traditional media gatekeepers would not have distributed. Streaming services commission content for diverse audience segments that broadcast TV, seeking mass audiences, would not serve. But the digital divide means not everyone benefits.
